extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and evaluative criteria for inductive reasoning, the law of causation, natural classification, and related logical/probabilistic judgments as presented in a philosophy-of-science textbook excerpt. Focuses on what induction requires, how to treat uniformity, classification of Kinds, and related fallacies and definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of uniformity required for induction
rubrics_metrics.description: The induction that 'fire burns' does not require that all nature observe uniform laws, but only that there should be uniformity in one particular class of natural phenomena (e.g. effects of fire on the senses and combustible substances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniformity needed is limited to the class of phenomena under observation; one does not need to assume a universal, all-pervading principle of uniformity prior to experience—the observed instances that establish the narrower truth also establish as much of the wider truth as corresponds to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of nature as empirical conclusion, not an a priori principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformity to the extent required for induction is not assumed anterior to experience but proved by experience; the law of causation is not thereby known a priori but is a conclusion from observed regularities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticisms that treat the law of causation as intuition or transcendental (e.g., Taine, Dr. Ward) are addressed: abstractions do not provide evidence of universal objective facts beyond what experience shows; the limitations of testimony cannot be cast off in abstract interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional status of scientific truths
rubrics_metrics.description: When physical science is said to depend on the assumption that the course of nature is invariable, the conclusions of physical science are not absolute truths but conditional on the uniformity of nature; observations and experiments prove that results are true if, and as long as, present laws remain valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conditional conclusiveness is sufficient for guidance in life; transcendental proofs do not practically strengthen this assurance (Dr. Ward's position discussed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracles interpreted as cases involving new antecedent causes, not breaches of causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Alleged miracles are not exceptions to the law of causation because in every case of alleged miracle a new antecedent—a counteracting cause, namely the volition of a supernatural being—is affirmed to exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To those who accept superhuman agents as vera causa, miracles exemplify the law of universal causation rather than deviations from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between uniformity of nature and universality of causation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no other uniformity in the events of nature than that which arises from the law of causation; if uniformity of the course of nature has exceptions, to that extent the law of causation fails—there would be events which do not depend on causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes the law of causation from mere long-continued uniformity; universality of causation is tied to uniform sequences of special effects from natural agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for identifying natural Kinds: conjunction of properties
rubrics_metrics.description: A Kind is commonly identified by several properties taken together; each property singly is often joint to other Kinds. (Example: diamond is identified by color, brightness, and octahedral form together, plus other ascertained properties and indefinite others unascertained.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some Kinds may be sufficiently identified by one remarkable property, but generally multiple properties are required; allotropic forms of the same chemical substance are treated as different Kinds in this sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of the Canons of Induction to chemical composition and special sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements about chemical composition (e.g., water composed of hydrogen and oxygen) are cases of causation and therefore fall under the Canons of Induction; special sciences may require adaptations of inductive methods, but these are particular applications of general logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special adaptations belong to the logic of the special sciences (e.g., chemistry) and are appropriate subjects for those who treat these sciences specifically (cf. Professor Bain).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on inference from approximate generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: From two approximate generalizations such as 'Most A are B' and 'Most A are C' the utmost certain conclusion is that 'some B are C.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approximate generalizations with unknown degrees of approximation cannot warrant stronger universal conclusions; this is the limit when the precise degree of approximation is undefined (De Morgan remark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct method for combining probabilistic generalizations (causal-grounded probabilities)
rubrics_metrics.description: The true theory of chances for combined generalizations should be grounded in the scientific (causal) grounds on which the proportions rest: the frequency of a coincidence depends on the frequency combined with the efficacy of causes favorable to it, not on naive multiplicative application suited to reverse problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example analysis: if among As 8/12 are Bs and among Cs 9/12 are Bs, when considering items that are both As and Cs, the combined operation of both sets of causes yields 11/12 Bs (six by both causes, two by A-causes only, three by C-causes only, one none). Avoid applying a calculation intended for the reverse problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of impossibility tied to complete induction
rubrics_metrics.description: An impossibility is that the truth of which would conflict with a complete induction, i.e., with the most conclusive evidence we possess of universal truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition encompasses logical impossibilities (e.g., 2+2=5, two straight lines enclosing a space) and causal impossibilities (e.g., things for which there exists no adequate cause). Many supposed impossibilities based only on present ignorance (e.g., fast travel, painless surgery, instantaneous telecommunication in earlier times) are not permanently incredible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred geometric definition of parallelism: equidistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Parallel lines are better characterized by the property of being everywhere equally distant (equidistance) rather than merely 'in the same plane and never meeting.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equidistance more accurately captures the meaning 'lines pursuing exactly the same direction' and obviates the need to assume additional axioms that arise from defining parallels only as coplanar non-intersecting lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of inappropriate (and false) conceptions in scientific explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying an inappropriate conception (a general law not corresponding to facts) to explain phenomena leads to failure; sometimes the conception is not just inappropriate but false—having no prototype in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (Whewell): using 'properties of the circle' to explain lever mechanics, assuming circular quality of sun's light to explain luminous spots, or assuming likeness between elements and compound to explain composition—these are errors beyond wrong choice of principle, they misassume matters of fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition that empirical generalizations point to higher causal laws rather than being ultimate
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical regularities (e.g., relation between atomic weight and specific heat; specific gravity and atomic weights in gases) have the appearance of pointing to higher laws and causal explanations rather than being ultimate laws themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such generalizations may be explained by deeper causal mechanisms (e.g., molecular motions), and apparent anomalies may be due to mistaken measurements (e.g., miscounting atoms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of specific formal fallacies in reasoning (à dicto secundum quid, fallacia accidentis, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware of logical fallacies such as à dicto secundum quid ad dictum simpliciter (overgeneralizing a qualified statement) and its converse (fallacia accidentis); these are common errors in argument and can be illustrated by everyday examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult treatments (e.g., De Morgan's chapter on Fallacies) for apt instances and remedies; the text shows how these forms of fallacious transfer of qualifiers lead to erroneous conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating testimony and event-credibility by combining event frequencies and witness reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing the credibility of a reported event, one must consider both the objective frequency of the event and the reliability (veracity) of the witness; naive comparisons can misstate relative credibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (note on drawing balls): with witness veracity 9/10 and different base frequencies for rare vs common events, compute credibilities by combining the true occurrence counts and false-announcement counts to obtain correct ratios (illustrates why naive multiplicative intuition may fail).
